m1_forms.back: Offensive speechLanguage targeting someone's identity, appearance, or performance with the intention of humiliating, insulting, or degrading them.
Digital hostilityHarmful behavior directed at a person or group through repeated or coordinated negative online interactions, such as mass reporting or collective harassment.
Hate speechHostile or malicious language targeting someone because of a protected characteristic, including race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, or disability.

m2_affected.back: AthletesHigh public visibility can make athletes frequent targets of online abuse. Abuse may follow a loss, a mistake, a performance, or a personal decision, and harmful content can quickly spread across digital platforms.

Match officialsOfficials can face online abuse following decisions made during competition, adding to the verbal and physical abuse they may already experience in person. Repeated criticism, threats, and hostility can contribute to stress and affect their confidence, perceived authority, and wellbeing.

JournalistsJournalists play an important role in connecting athletes, teams, and sporting organisations with wider audiences. Coverage perceived as critical or negative can lead to online hostility from fans, athletes, teams, and others engaging with their work.

Sponsors and representativesSporting organisations and the people who fund, manage, and represent them can also become targets of online abuse. Hostile content may be directed at an organisation itself, its decisions or actions, or at individual staff and representatives. This can affect organisational reputation, professional activity, decision-making, and the wellbeing of those involved.

FamiliesThe effects of online abuse can extend to the families and loved ones of those targeted. They may witness the abuse and its impact, receive harmful messages themselves as indirect targets, or experience increased concern and fear for the safety and wellbeing of someone close to them.

FansFans are the largest group in sport and are often overlooked. They can be affected by the abuse they encounter within sporting communities, even when they are not its direct target. Identity-based abuse aimed at an athlete, official, or other public figure can also affect fans who share that identity, contributing to an environment in which they may feel unwelcome or unsafe.

m3_checklist: 1. Assess the situation and your safety. Consider the nature of the content and whether you or someone else may be at immediate risk.
2. Collect evidence. Save abusive posts, messages, profile information, URLs, and screenshots where appropriate.
3. Record key details. Note the date, time, username or account, and relevant information about what occurred.
4. Use platform safety tools. Restrict, mute, or block the account where appropriate to limit further contact or exposure.
5. Report through the platform. Review the platform’s relevant policies and flag the content or account using its built-in reporting options.

6. Seek additional support or escalate when needed. Contact your organisation’s welfare or safeguarding lead where relevant. If you feel there is a threat to your safety, contact the appropriate local authorities or emergency services.

m4_tabs.title: Criminal law
m4_tabs.html:
What it can cover: Conduct that constitutes a criminal offence under the applicable law, which may include certain threats, stalking, hate crimes, or non-consensual sharing of intimate images.

Who takes action: Law enforcement may investigate, and the relevant prosecuting authority determines whether a case proceeds.

Possible outcomes: Criminal penalties can include fines or imprisonment, depending on the offence and jurisdiction.

See an example

Following a controversial decision during a match, a referee begins receiving repeated messages in his social media from the same account. The messages become increasingly threatening and include references to seriously harming the referee and members of their family. Depending on the applicable law and circumstances, threats of this nature could lead to a report to law enforcement and a criminal investigation.

m4_tabs.title: Civil law
m4_tabs.html:
What it can cover: Disputes involving legal rights between individuals or organisations, which may include defamation, harassment, misuse of private information, or other privacy-related claims.

Who takes action: The person or organisation bringing the claim initiates the legal process.

Possible outcomes: Depending on the applicable law, remedies can include compensation or court orders requiring particular conduct to stop.

See an example

False allegations about an athlete begin circulating online and are repeatedly shared. The claims damage the athlete’s professional reputation, and a sponsor ends its relationship with them after seeing such allegations. Depending on the applicable law and circumstances, the athlete may be able to bring a civil claim seeking a remedy for the harm caused.

m4_tabs.title: Administrative law and regulation
m4_tabs.html:
What it can cover: Legal obligations enforced by regulators, including rules applying to online services or the handling of personal data.

Who takes action: Relevant regulatory authorities oversee and enforce these requirements. Individuals and organisations may also be able to submit complaints.

Possible outcomes: Regulators may investigate, require changes, or impose penalties where the applicable law gives them those powers.

See an example

An athlete discovers that their personal contact information has been published online without their permission. The information continues to circulate, creating concerns about their privacy and safety. Depending on the applicable data protection rules, the athlete or their organisation may be able to raise the matter with the relevant regulatory authority.

m4_accordion.title: United Kingdom
m4_accordion.html:
In the UK, several laws can apply to harmful online conduct depending on the circumstances. The Online Safety Act 2023, for example, includes offences concerning threatening communications and sharing or threatening to share certain intimate images without consent. Existing harassment and stalking offences can also apply to relevant conduct.

Source: Legislation.gov.uk

m4_accordion.title: United States
m4_accordion.html:
In the United States, both federal and state laws may apply. Federal law, for example, addresses certain stalking conduct involving electronic or online communications when its statutory requirements are met. State laws can provide additional protections, so the applicable rules depend on the circumstances and jurisdiction.

Source: U.S. Code

m4_accordion.title: Czechia
m4_accordion.html:
Czechia law does not rely on a single offence of “online abuse”. Existing legislation can apply to specific harmful behaviours carried out online. For example, the Czech Criminal Code addresses stalking, including conduct carried out through electronic communications. Czech Police guidance explicitly recognises cyberstalking and identifies repeated social media messages, threats, misuse of personal data, and reputational attacks among behaviours that may occur in stalking cases.

The Czech Civil Code (Act No. 89/2012 Coll.) also protects personality rights, including a person’s dignity, honour and privacy. A person affected by unlawful interference can seek to have the interference stopped and its consequences remedied.

Source: e-Sbírka

m4_accordion.title: Spain
m4_accordion.html:
Spain’s Criminal Code specifically addresses several behaviours that can occur through digital platforms. Its stalking provisions cover repeated unwanted contact through any means of communication and also address the misuse of someone’s personal data. Spanish law also specifically covers the non-consensual use of a person’s image to create fake social-media profiles when this causes harassment or humiliation.

Spain also gives particular legal attention to some forms of online hate speech: penalties can be increased when certain hate-related offences are committed through the internet or information technologies in a way that makes the content accessible to a large number of people.

Source: Gobierno de España

m4_accordion.title: Sweden
m4_accordion.html:
In Sweden, online hate or abuse is not a separate legal category. The Swedish Police explains that the same criminal laws generally apply to conduct online as they do offline, with relevant offences potentially including unlawful threats, harassment, defamation, insult, unlawful invasion of privacy, sexual harassment, and agitation against a population group.

Swedish law also recognises unlawful persecution, which can arise from repeated criminal acts against the same person. Police guidance specifically advises people experiencing stalking to preserve emails, text messages, call records and other digital communications as potential evidence.

Sources: polisen.se; Swedish Parliament

m4_accordion.title: Slovenia
m4_accordion.html:
Slovenian law addresses online abuse through existing legislation covering specific harmful behaviours. A particularly relevant example is Article 134a of the Slovenian Criminal Code (KZ-1), which defines stalking to include repeated attempts to establish unwanted contact through electronic communications, where the conduct causes fear or a sense of threat. Slovenian authorities have also recognised the online dimension of stalking in guidance concerning the application of this provision.

Slovenian Police guidance recognises online violence as including behaviours such as threats, harassment, spreading false or insulting content, misuse of photographs, impersonation and the creation of harmful fake profiles. Whether particular conduct constitutes a criminal offence depends on the circumstances of the individual case.

Source: GOV.SI

steps.title: Protect yourself
steps.content:
1 — Protect yourself

For athletes and others with public-facing roles:

  • Manage your exposure. Review privacy and safety settings and control who can contact, mention, or tag you.
  • Use safety tools. Mute, restrict, block, and report harmful accounts or content.
  • Preserve evidence. Save relevant information when behaviour may need to be reported or escalated.
  • Protect your wellbeing. Step away when needed and seek support from people you trust.
Why does this matter?

Protecting yourself is part of the collective response. When people use safety and wellbeing tools, they are better equipped to prevent harm within the wider sporting community.

steps.title: Support others
steps.content:
2 — Support others

As a teammate, colleague, fan, friend, or bystander:

  • Avoid amplification. Do not repost abusive content, including when condemning it.
  • Check in privately. Let the person targeted know they have support.
  • Report appropriately. Use platform or organisational reporting channels.
  • Speak up safely. Challenge harmful behaviour when it is appropriate and safe to do so.
Why does this matter?

Supporting others strengthens the sporting community. Small actions from teammates, colleagues, friends, fans, and other bystanders can help create a social support system where people feel heard, protected, and cared for, and harmful behaviour is less likely to go unchallenged.

steps.title: Act safely
steps.content:
3 — Act safely

When responding to online abuse, consider the situation, personal safety, and whether additional support is needed:

  • Assess the situation. Consider the nature of the behaviour, whether it is escalating, and whether anyone may be at risk.
  • Avoid unsafe engagement. Do not confront or engage directly when doing so could increase harm or place someone at risk.
  • Know when to seek support. Involve a trusted person or the appropriate organisational contact when the situation requires additional help.
  • Escalate safety concerns. Threats, repeated unwanted contact, exposure of personal information, or other safety concerns may require further organisational or external support.
Why does this matter?

Acting safely helps connect individual action with the right level of support. Recognising when a situation requires additional help allows others to become involved and helps ensure that safety remains the priority.

steps.title: Prepare
steps.content:
1 — Prepare

Develop policies and codes of conduct, provide education and training, and establish clear expectations for digital behaviour.

steps.title: Protect
steps.content:
2 — Protect

Provide welfare and safeguarding support, platform safety tools, moderation, and appropriate mechanisms for people at risk.

steps.title: Respond
steps.content:
3 — Respond

Create accessible reporting pathways, preserve appropriate records, apply organisational procedures, and coordinate escalation when necessary.

steps.title: Connect
steps.content:
4 — Connect

Work with other organisations, platforms, authorities, researchers, advocacy groups, and specialist services when a response extends beyond the organisation’s own capabilities.

steps.title: Stronger together
steps.content:
5 — Stronger together

Organisations are stronger when they work together. Clubs can provide frontline support, federations set shared standards, platforms enable reporting and moderation, media organisations manage published content, and advocacy groups may contribute with specialised support and education. Together, they can create a coordinated network of protection and response against online abuse.

steps.title: Education
steps.content:
1 — Education

Education can help people recognise online abuse, understand its consequences, and know how to respond safely. Digital and media literacy can also strengthen critical thinking about what behaviours are appropriate in online settings.

steps.title: Shared standards
steps.content:
2 — Shared standards

Clear expectations help establish which behaviours are considered acceptable within sporting communities. Shared standards around respect, inclusion, fair play, and digital participation can guide behaviour and give individuals and organisations a stronger basis for challenging abuse.

steps.title: Research and evidence
steps.content:
3 — Research and evidence

Evidence and data-driven research help map the patterns where online abuse occurs, how harmful behaviour evolves in time, and which responses are more effective. Stronger knowledge can inform prevention, education, organisational practice, technology, and policy.

steps.title: Policy and law
steps.content:
4 — Policy and law

Policies and laws can establish boundaries, responsibilities, protections, and routes to accountability. They can influence behaviour by clarifying consequences and providing mechanisms for reporting, intervention, and redress.

steps.title: Technology and platform design
steps.content:
5 — Technology and platform design

The design of digital platforms can influence how easily harmful content is created, discovered, amplified, reported, or removed. Moderation, detection, reporting tools, and other safety features can help reduce opportunities for abuse to spread and persist.

steps.title: Community norms
steps.content:
6 — Community norms

Social norms influence what people perceive as normal, acceptable, or worth challenging. Athletes, fans, media, organisations, and public figures all contribute to the culture surrounding sport. When communities consistently challenge abusive behaviour and reinforce respect, they can help shift the norms that allow online abuse to persist.

steps.title: Working together
steps.content:
7 — Working together

These factors work together across sport and in our society. Education can shape how people understand online behaviours, while shared standards and laws can clarify expectations, research can identify emerging risks, and technology can influence how harmful content spreads.

Sporting communities are only a part of our society: they are influenced by broader cultural norms, and athletes, fans, media, organisations, and other voices in sport can also help shape the world we live in together.
